canonicalization: SHA256 of UTF-8 JSON payload with keys recursively sorted, separators=(',',':'), ensure_ascii=false; digest covers payload only

classification_contract.HARD_STABLE_INVARIANT: Exact/per-instance/version-bound value is stable through healthy normal operation and its unexpected change creates a concrete upgrade-safety or compatibility risk. Mismatch stops mutation until an explicit supported migration/version transition is selected.
classification_contract.SOFT_RUNTIME_CHECK: Do not require historical equality. Evaluate a semantic predicate/range/supported set. An unsafe result may stop or defer mutation, but a benign value change is allowed.
classification_contract.DIAGNOSTIC_ONLY: Collect/retain for troubleshooting or evidence correlation; never block an upgrade by this field alone.
classification_contract.REMOVE: Exclude from the future A2 updater gate/normal observer because it is historical-only, redundant, or an obsolete aggregate. Frozen historical evidence remains unchanged.

entries.reason: Repository source head is useful provenance, but docs/tools-only commits can change it without changing the deployed product. Gate the actual approved image/runtime contract instead.
R2A control-plane head is historical experiment provenance, not a live product contract. Preserve it only in frozen reference evidence.
R2B control-plane head is historical experiment provenance, not a live product contract. Preserve it only in frozen reference evidence.
Historical R2A transaction bytes must not become a permanent runtime gate after the transaction is terminal and archived.
Historical R2B transaction bytes are not a current product invariant; the public gap must not trigger destructive recreation or future upgrade blocking.
The approved Broker image is part of the module identity. An unexpected image means the updater cannot prove which code/config contract it is about to mutate.
The production artifact is built for the approved platform. A platform mismatch can make image execution or rollback unsafe.
This binds the Broker launch contract such as user, network mode, mounts, security options and port bindings. Silent drift can weaken security or break persistence/listener behavior.
The approved Home Assistant image is a module identity input. Unexpected code means compatibility and rollback assumptions are no longer proven.
Home Assistant must run on the supported production platform; a mismatch invalidates the frozen artifact/runtime assumptions.
The runtime contract binds mounts, network and security properties that protect /config persistence and MQTT/HTTP behavior.
Manager image identity must be explicit for each baseline/target. The R3 A->b863 change proves the value may change only through an authorized version transition, not ordinary runtime drift.
Manager artifact compatibility depends on the supported platform; mismatch makes execution and rollback assumptions unsafe.
Manager mounts, host-network use, runtime user and security settings are part of the supported module contract. Silent drift can break MQTT, persistence or credential ownership.
A whole-Compose byte hash crosses module boundaries and would over-couple independent upgrades. A2 should gate each module by its runtime/config contract instead.
The Broker fixed configuration defines listener, TLS and Dynamic Security behavior. Unexpected byte drift can change exposure or authentication semantics.
The fixed N3-W Home Assistant configuration is part of the supported integration contract; unplanned drift can break MQTT/bootstrap behavior.
n3w_mqtt_bootstrap code is part of the Home Assistant product integration. Unexpected tree drift changes product behavior without a declared HA/module version transition.
Exact unit-file bytes belong to the host/operations layer, not T1_Core_Stack module identity. A2 should check required unit semantics/state, not exact historical file hashes.

Persistent paths must remain the expected object type and be owned by the service identity that must read/write them. Unexpected ownership/type drift can cause data loss, startup failure or unsafe writes.
Permissions must remain safe and usable, but a stricter valid mode can differ from the historical exact value. Gate by allowed permission policy, not byte-for-byte mode equality.
Database integrity must be healthy before mutation, but this is a runtime health predicate rather than product identity.
Schema version may intentionally advance during a supported migration. The updater must require a supported/migratable value rather than historical equality.

The exact current schema is stable during normal operation and determines whether a migration/rollback is safe. A2 may allow an explicit set of predecessor/target schema hashes, but unknown schema must stop mutation.
Table count is a weak derivative of schema identity and adds no safety signal once the schema hash/version are checked.
The FC4 private CA is the trust anchor used by Broker/Manager/nodes and is not replaced during ordinary server-certificate renewal. Unexpected change can break fleet TLS trust.
The Broker server certificate is lifecycle-managed and may be renewed while remaining valid under the same CA and hostname contract. Exact certificate bytes must not be a permanent gate.
System CA is persistent greenhouse identity/recovery material. Rotation must be an explicit trust-migration operation, not ordinary module-runtime drift.
The Dynamic Security document structure is part of Broker authentication compatibility. Unknown structural drift can make authorization parsing or rollback unsafe.
The host must be in an acceptable operating state before/after an upgrade, but exact historical state text is runtime health rather than product identity.
This is redundant with the failed-unit list. A2 should inspect relevant failed units directly instead of maintaining two gates for the same fact.
Current failed units matter to upgrade safety, but policy should distinguish relevant product/host failures from unrelated historical exact equality.
Required activation/guard/timer semantics must be healthy, but service state is a runtime condition and some units are intentionally quiescent.
The three product services should be present when the stack is converged, but running-service presence is a runtime health condition, not immutable artifact identity.
Manager must authenticate to Broker for normal operation. This is a minimum post-upgrade product-health behavior.
Home Assistant must authenticate to Broker for normal operation; this is runtime health, not product identity.
Exact live socket count can change transiently and is explicitly disqualified from hard equality. Authentication/functional continuity are stronger gates.
Exact Home Assistant MQTT socket count is runtime-variable and should not gate by historical equality.
HTTP availability is required after convergence, but multiple statuses such as 200/401 can be valid; use an allowed semantic set.
This aggregate bakes old observer assumptions, including exact socket-count rules. Keeping it would preserve the very over-gating A1 is meant to remove.
Boot identity necessarily changes after reboot and is useful only to correlate evidence within one boot.
Container instance ID, start time and historical restart count are runtime history; healthy restart/recreate changes them.
Manager container instance history changes during an authorized Manager upgrade and must not become a stable gate.
Home Assistant container instance history can change during service-group restart even when HA code is unchanged; retain only for forensic timing.
This duplicates the Manager socket count already exposed in health and adds no independent upgrade-safety information.
Connection fingerprint and historical authentication-event count change across reconnects and are useful for forensics, not gating.
Manager MQTT username/client identity is provisioned persistent identity. Unexpected change without coordinated credential/DynSec migration can break authentication or bind the wrong principal.
This duplicates the Home Assistant socket count already exposed in health.
Connection fingerprint and authentication-event history change with reconnects and service restarts.
Home Assistant MQTT identity must remain bound to the intended principal unless a coordinated credential/DynSec migration is explicitly performed.
Business rows legitimately grow/change with registrations, telemetry and replay history. Counts are useful diagnostics but must not block ordinary upgrades by historical equality.
Database and WAL sizes vary with normal use, checkpoints and compaction; exact values are not product identity.
Persistent trees naturally grow and shrink with normal product operation; these values are capacity/forensic signals only.
Unexpected symlinks can make backup/restore or mutation follow unintended paths. Check a safety policy, but do not assume exact historical tree equality.
Client count changes with node population, and group/role counts alone are too weak to prove authorization semantics. They should not gate by exact count.
Required HA registry documents should exist in a converged installation, but this is a runtime/storage health predicate.
Entity/device/config-entry counts legitimately change with discovery and customer use.
Home Assistant may migrate storage versions. The updater should require a supported/understood version, not exact equality to the clean reference.
